query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys reported to date commonly contain both solid solutions and intermetallic compounds. Induction-melted Al- and Mg-rich alloys reached densities of 2.64–2.75 g/cm3 but all had complex structures; Al20Be20Fe10Si15Ti35 combined a density of 3.91 g/cm3 with 911 HV hardness and oxidation resistance at 700 and 900 °C; compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd showed region-dependent compression, plasticity, and corrosion behavior; and reported AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys contained a primary BCC constituent together with intermetallic compounds, with x = 1.0 showing the best property combination in that series. Prior studies have emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, whereas interfacial segregation, interfacial energy, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance remain insufficiently studied. The design must retain a density below 6 g/cm3 and address performance constraints associated with the tendency of Mg and dissimilar constituent elements to form stable intermetallic compounds. Starting from an as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state, what single intervention hypothesis could improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance? State the intervention, its proposed causal mechanism, quantitative or directional predictions relative to the as-processed baseline, the composition and operating or test boundaries, the prior experimental evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with explicit observations that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of Cr into the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy can improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state
generation.conditions: Processing conditions similar to those used for the WVTaTiCr x alloy coatings
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense oxide film and refinement of grain structure
generation.mechanism: The addition of Cr causes more severe lattice distortion, opening a path for atomic diffusion and promoting the precipitation of intermetallic compounds, which can improve the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of the alloy. The dense oxide film formed can inhibit oxygen diffusion, reducing the oxidation rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical properties, including yield strength and hardness, as well as enhanced corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation resistance
generation.baseline: As-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy without Cr addition
generation.boundary: Alloy composition range: Mg-rich with varying Cr content; processing conditions: similar to those used for the WVTaTiCr x alloy coatings
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Cr required to achieve optimal properties is uncertain and may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with varying Cr content and evaluate their mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Cr does not result in improved mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance, the hypothesis is falsified.

System: WVTaTiCr x (x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings on 42-CrMo steel substrate. Processing: Laser cladding using a LYHS series ultra-high-speed laser-cladding machine; powder mixture of W, V, Ta, Ti, Cr (45–105 μm, 99.9% purity) ball-milled for 24 h at 300 r/min (10:1 ball-to-material ratio); laser power 1.4 kW, scanning speed 8 mm/s, spot diameter 6 mm, overlap rate 30–40%, argon protective gas. Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite processing challenges, and how do its microstructure, hardness, and corrosion resistance compare to traditional superalloys and arc-melted counterparts?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition of Nb, Mo, Ta, W powders with 99.9% purity). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); parameters included hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, and a triple-pass remelting strategy (3x energy input) to achieve a linear energy density of 2.83 J/mm.
